text: I am a storyteller. <break time="0.8s" /> And I would like to tell you a few personal stories about what I like to call the danger of the single story. <break time="0.8s" /> I grew up on a university campus in eastern Nigeria. <break time="0.8s" /> My mother says that I started reading at the age of two, although I think four is probably closer to the truth. <break time="0.8s" /> So I was an early reader. <break time="0.8s" /> And what I read were British and American childrens books. <break time="0.8s" /> I was also an early writer. <break time="0.8s" /> And when I began to write, at about the age of seven, stories in pencil with crayon illustrations that my poor mother was obligated to read, I wrote exactly the kinds of stories I was reading. <break time="0.8s" /> All my characters were white and blue eyed. <break time="0.8s" /> They played in the snow. <break time="0.8s" /> They ate apples. <break time="0.8s" /> And they talked a lot about the weather, how lovely it was that the sun had come out. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, this was despite the fact that I lived in Nigeria. <break time="0.8s" /> I had never been outside Nigeria. <break time="0.8s" /> We did not have snow. <break time="0.8s" /> We ate mangoes. <break time="0.8s" /> And we never talked about the weather, because there was no need to. <break time="0.8s" /> My characters also drank a lot of ginger beer, because the characters in the British books I read drank ginger beer. <break time="0.8s" /> Never mind that I had no idea what ginger beer was. <break time="0.8s" /> And for many years afterwards, I would have a desperate desire to taste ginger beer. <break time="0.8s" /> But that is another story. <break time="0.8s" /> What this demonstrates, I think, is how impressionable and vulnerable we are in the face of a story, particularly as children.
